title: Kandu's Nine Hundred Years
hook: a sage hurries to his evening prayer, nine centuries late
carry: sandhya: prayer at the turning of the day
tomorrow: the worst age of the world is the best one? who says that?

segments.voice: Yesterday, more of the Vishnu Purana, the book these days have been dipping into one story at a time. Today's story starts in the middle of an evening.

The phone says nine. You look again and it says one in the morning, and nothing in between felt like four hours. The Vishnu Purana has a sage this happens to, on a much bigger scale. His name is Kandu. One evening he jumps up in a hurry: the sun is going down, and it's time for his evening prayers by the river. The woman he lives with, Pramlocha, watches him go and stops him with one question. Evening prayers? For which evening?
screen: `NINE O'CLOCK. THEN ONE.` → `A SAGE JUMPS UP AT SUNSET.` → `FOR WHICH EVENING?`

segments.voice: Here's how he got there. Kandu was a sage of great tapas, the heat of hard practice, living by the river Gomati. Indra, king of the gods, was uneasy at that much power, so he sent Pramlocha, a dancer of heaven, to break Kandu's concentration. It worked. The two of them went to live in a lovely valley, and the days were sweet. Now and then she asked to go back to heaven, and each time he asked her to stay a little longer. Then that evening. He's hurrying off to his evening rite, and she tells him the truth: by her count, more than nine hundred years have gone by. He's shaken, and his sharpest words are for himself: all that practice, spent. He sends her away and goes off to worship Vishnu, back to the practice he had left. Now notice what woke him: the evening prayer. Its name is sandhya, the joining, the moment one part of the day turns into the next. Traditional Hindu practice keeps prayer at those joints, dawn and dusk above all. Many who keep the old rite say the Gayatri there, and many homes still light a lamp at sunset. Many teachers read Kandu's story as a picture of life without those joints: nothing wicked, just one sweet evening that never turned. The sandhya is the tradition's answer. Stop where the day turns, and remember God.
screen: `TAPAS BY THE RIVER GOMATI.` · `SENT BY INDRA: PRAMLOCHA.` · `NINE HUNDRED YEARS, ONE EVENING.` · `SANDHYA: WHERE THE DAY TURNS.` · then, large: `STOP WHERE THE DAY TURNS. REMEMBER GOD.`

segments.voice: Whatever time it is, treat this as a turning of the day. If you pray, light a lamp or face the light, and say a name of God, or the Gayatri if you know it, slowly. If you don't pray, say out loud what part of the day this is, then sit and notice the turning: the light, the sounds, your own breath. That's a small sandhya, a stop at the joint.
The Vishnu Purana. Today's story from it: Kandu, whose evening prayer woke him nine centuries late.
Your line: sandhya, prayer at the turning of the day. Kandu's evening never turned; yours can. See you tomorrow.
